newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala rebel disarmament to begin in March.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala rebel disarmament to begin in March.

text.p: Hundreds of Guatemalan guerrilla fighters will begin moving into disarmament camps on March 3 as part of a U.N.-brokered peace accord that recently ended a 36-year civil war, officials said on Friday.

"We've been able to fix that date because camp construction is well under way and because (U.N.) military observers have begun to arrive," said David Stephen, director of the U.N. mission for Human Rights Verification in Guatemala.
A mission of 155 unarmed United Nations observers, so-called "blue berets," will oversee disarmament at each of eight camps in six rural areas around the country during March and April.

More than three decades of civil war ended in this Central American nation on Dec. 29 when the government and leftist rebels of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) signed a historic peace treaty.
Rebel disarmament is one aspect of 11 complex and comprehensive accords in the peace agreement, which includes social programmes and Indian rights.

The Guatemalan army, which earned a reputation for rampant human rights violations during 36 years of counter-insurgency campaigns, will shrink by one third and abandon its state police role under peace terms.

The United Nations moderated Guatemalan peace talks, but the organisation's participation in disarmament was thrown into doubt in January when China used its veto power in the U.N. Security Council to block the "blue beret" mission.

China withdrew its veto after two weeks of diplomatic wrangling and U.N. Gen. Jose Rodriguez arrived on Feb. 5 to oversee construction of the camps, which include rudimentary housing, latrines, drinking water and soccer fields.
Rodriguez, who is supervising the observation mission, said rebels will not move to the camps until the military has made a goodwill gesture and removed any installations near camps.
By Feb. 17, the URNG must turn in official lists of how many guerrillas will be moving to the camps and what weapons will be turned in, Rodriguez said.
The URNG has said 3,000-4,000 guerrillas will gather in the camps, but the camps are designed to house some 2,500 people.
Rodriguez said the government and the URNG will decide whether weapons will be destroyed.

The ex-guerrillas must leave the camps, mostly constructed on land rented from farmers and ranchers, after May 3. Programmes, such as job training to help guerrillas return to civilian life, will begin in the camps.
